result.topic_en: Euler works out the general equation for the special cases m = 1, 2, 3, where the order exponent is n+m. In each case he reduces it to an explicit relation between a finite power sum in q and a multiple of a power of p.
result.transcription:
SERIES SINGVLARES. 171
28. Antequam ad ordines ſupra conſideratos deſcendamus, euoluamus in genere aliquos caſus.
I. Sit igitur $m = 1$ et aequatio inuenta induet hanc formam:
$0 = q - q^{n} - q^{n-1} - q^{n-2} \dots\dots - q + n p^{n+1}$
ſeu $q^{2} + q^{3} + q^{4} \dots\dots + q^{n} = n p^{n+1}$
exponente ordinis exiſtente $n+1$, ita vt ſit
$q^{\mu} + q^{n+1-\mu} = p^{\mu} + p^{n-1}$.
II. Sit $m = 2$, ordinisque exponens $n+2$, vt ſit $q^{\mu} + q^{n+2-\mu} = p^{\mu} + p^{n+2}$ et aequatio noſtra fiet
$0 = q^{2} - n(q + q^{n+1}) + q^{n} + 2q^{n-1} + 3q^{n-2} + 4q^{n-3} \dots + nq$
$+ n p^{n+2} \qquad - \frac{n(n+1)}{1 \cdot 2} p^{n+2}$
ſiue
$q^{n} + 2q^{n-1} + 3q^{n-2} \dots (n-1)q^{2} - nq^{n+1} = \frac{n(n-1)}{1 \cdot 2} p^{n+2}$.
III. Sit $m = 3$, ordinisque exponens $n+3$, vt ſit $q^{\mu} + q^{n+3-\mu} = p^{\mu} + p^{n+3}$ et aequatio noſtra erit
$0 = q^{3} - n(q^{2} + q^{n+1}) + \frac{n(n+1)}{1 \cdot 2}(q + q^{n+2})$
$- \frac{n(n-1)}{1 \cdot 2} p^{n+3}$
$- q^{n} - 3q^{n-1} - 6q^{n-2} - 10q^{n-3} \dots\dots - \frac{n(n+1)}{1 \cdot 2} q$
$+ \frac{n(n+1)(n+2)}{1 \cdot 2 \cdot 3} p^{n+3}$
ſiue
$q^{n} + 3q^{n-1} + 6q^{n-2} \dots\dots + \frac{(n-1)(n-2)}{1 \cdot 2} q^{3} + \frac{n(n-1)}{1 \cdot 2} q^{2} + n q^{n+1}$
$= \frac{n(nn+5)}{6} p^{n+3} \qquad -1 \qquad +n \qquad - \frac{n(n+1)}{1 \cdot 2} q^{n+2}$
vel hoc modo diſtinctius:
$q^{n} + 3q^{n-1} + 6q^{n-2} + 10q^{n-3} \dots\dots + \frac{n(n-1)}{1 \cdot 2} q^{2}$
$- q^{3} + n(q^{2} + q^{n+1}) - \frac{n(n+1)}{1 \cdot 2} q^{n+2} = \frac{n(nn+5)}{6} p^{n+3}$.
Y 2 \qquad IV.

items.quote: Antequam ad ordines ſupra conſideratos deſcendamus, euoluamus in genere aliquos caſus.
items.english: Before we descend to the orders considered above, let us work out some cases in general.

items.quote: ſeu $q^{2} + q^{3} + q^{4} \dots\dots + q^{n} = n p^{n+1}$
items.english: For m = 1 (order exponent n+1), the equation becomes q^2 + q^3 + ... + q^n = n p^{n+1}.
For m = 2 (order exponent n+2), the equation reduces to q^n + 2q^{n-1} + 3q^{n-2} + ... + (n-1)q^2 - n q^{n+1} = n(n-1)/2 · p^{n+2}.
For m = 3 (order exponent n+3), the equation is, more distinctly: q^n + 3q^{n-1} + 6q^{n-2} + 10q^{n-3} + ... + n(n-1)/2 · q^2 - q^3 + n(q^2 + q^{n+1}) - n(n+1)/2 · q^{n+2} = n(nn+5)/6 · p^{n+3}.
